# Fix, Focus, or Exit
## A Turnaround-or-Divestment Assessment and Plan for the Industrial-Services Unit

*Framework for unit leadership, group strategy, and the board. Follows the decision arc: diagnose, focus, prove, decide — under a one-year clock that is not a threat but a discipline. Three years of losses and two failed restructurings are not bad luck; they are data. The third plan cannot be a larger version of the first two.*

---

## Executive Summary

- **The diagnosis in one line:** two cost restructurings that left losses untouched demonstrate that the problem is not overhead — it is what work the unit does, for whom, and at what price. This plan therefore attacks portfolio and revenue quality before it touches cost again.
- **The method:** de-average the P&L to contract level, restate internal work at market prices, and separate a profitable core worth fighting for from a value-destroying tail to be exited. Fix the core; exit the tail. There is no third category.
- **The plan:** a one-year, four-gate turnaround with pre-agreed absolute thresholds, run in parallel with a small, firewalled exit-preparation track — so that a pivot to sale or wind-down at any gate is a gear-change, not a scramble.
- **The decision rule:** turnaround only if the focused core passes four tests — market, right-to-win, economics, execution capacity. Fail any one and the unit is divested or wound down, against criteria fixed in writing before the results arrive.
- **The ask of the board at kickoff:** sign the one-page charter (gate criteria, decision rights, month-12 exit expectations); appoint the turnaround lead and the board sponsor who owns the exit track; fund both tracks properly.

---

## 0. Operating Principles

1. **Two failed cost restructurings are the diagnosis's first clue.** Costs were cut and losses persisted — which means the problem lives in revenue quality, portfolio mix, or structural position, not in overhead. You cannot cut your way to profit on a deteriorating top line.
2. **De-average everything.** The blended P&L conceals a profitable core and a value-destroying tail. Every decision in this plan is made at the level of service line × customer segment × contract, never at unit level.
3. **Talent flight is a vote, and the voters have the best information.** The managers transferring out are the ones with options. Decode why they're leaving before writing the plan — and stop the outflow, because no plan survives the loss of the people meant to execute it.
4. **Evaluate everything at group level.** The unit serves customers of the profitable divisions. Its failure can damage relationships it doesn't own; its service capability may be worth more to the group than its standalone P&L shows. Every option — fix, sell, close — is priced including effects on sister divisions.
5. **Run turnaround and exit in parallel — and quietly.** The one-year clock forbids sequencing. Dual-track preparation preserves optionality and imposes buyer-grade discipline on the turnaround numbers. But a leaked sale process inside a fragile organization accelerates the very talent flight and customer defection that are already the unit's biggest problems. The exit track runs small, firewalled, and under a code name until a gate forces it open.
6. **Define "credible" before the results arrive.** Agree now, in writing, what a credible path to profitability looks like at each gate — measured against a restated baseline, with absolute thresholds. Otherwise the month-12 debate will be politics, not analysis — and sunk cost will argue for a fourth year.

---

## 1. Diagnostic — Structural or Execution?

### 1.1 The tests that distinguish them

| Test | Question | Evidence of structural failure | Evidence of execution failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Market** | Is the served market growing, flat, or declining? | End markets in secular decline; technology displacing the service | Market stable/growing; competitors adding capacity |
| **Relative economics** | Are competitors profitable in the same segments? | No one makes money; industry-wide margin collapse | Named competitors earn acceptable margins on comparable work |
| **Order book** | Why is it shrinking — lost bids, lost customers, or shrinking customer demand? | Customers' own demand is falling; work is being in-sourced or obsoleted | Win rates falling on bids we should win; churn to specific rivals |
| **Cost position** | Landed cost vs. competitors at equal scope | Structural disadvantage: scale, footprint, labor agreements, asset age | Utilization, scheduling, and rework problems — fixable with management |
| **Contract quality** | Where does margin leak? | Whole categories priced below cost by the market | Specific fixed-price jobs overrun; escalation clauses missing; pricing undisciplined |
| **Transfer pricing** | What does the P&L look like at market prices for work done for sister divisions? | — | Losses concentrated in internal work at non-market internal prices — an artifact, not a business failure |

### 1.2 Reading the known facts
- **Cost cuts that didn't touch losses** point to a revenue-mix or structural problem. The first question is not "where else can we cut" but "which work should we be doing at all."
- **A shrinking order book** is a demand-side signal. It must be decomposed: market decline (structural), competitive losses (execution — unless they persist for three years, in which case they usually reflect a structural disadvantage in scale, footprint, or capability), or deliberate low-ball bidding by rivals buying share.
- **Management flight** is both symptom and cause. It signals collapsed internal confidence and steadily erodes the execution capacity any turnaround depends on. Exit interviews with departed managers are a diagnostic instrument — use them.
- **The shared-customer overlap cuts both ways.** If the unit cannot profitably serve customers already buying from sister divisions, either execution is badly broken or the unit is being used as a margin sink for group deals at internal prices. Audit transfer pricing before concluding anything — the unit's "losses" may partly be an accounting artifact, and its true market-price economics may be better (or worse) than reported.

### 1.3 The diagnostic workplan (weeks 1–6, verdict at week 8)
- **Contract-level P&L:** rebuild three years of results contract by contract — price, cost, overruns, escalation terms. The order book gets the same treatment: which backlog is actually profitable at completion?
- **Win/loss and churn analysis** on 24 months of bids; interviews with the top 20 customers, including defectors.
- **Competitor benchmarking:** cost position, pricing, and profitability of two or three named rivals.
- **Transfer-pricing audit** of all work for sister divisions, restated at market rates — this restated P&L becomes the baseline for every gate metric in the plan.
- **Exit interviews** with every manager who transferred out in 24 months.
- **Preliminary verdict to the board at week 8.** A structural finding (Case C below) goes to the board then — not at Gate 1. No one burns four extra months confirming a verdict that is already clear.

### 1.4 The four possible verdicts
- **A — Healthy market, broken execution:** turnaround is credible; proceed to Section 3 in full.
- **B — Declining market, defensible niche:** shrink-to-profit — exit the broad market, concentrate on the protected niche.
- **C — Structural disadvantage, no right to win:** go directly to exit (Section 4). Do not burn nine months confirming it.
- **D — Mixed portfolio (the most likely):** fix the core, exit the tail — the plan below is built for this case.

## 2. Where Profit Can Live — Segments and Service Lines

### 2.1 Build the matrix
Construct a service-line × customer-segment profitability matrix at two levels: contribution margin and fully loaded cost, with internal work restated at market prices. Rank every cell. The plan concentrates on the top cells and exits the bottom ones — there is no third category.

### 2.2 Hypotheses to validate — where profit typically survives
- **Recurring-revenue service agreements** tied to an installed base — predictable, defensible, priced on value rather than bid.
- **Work for shared group customers at market pricing** — a channel advantage no competitor has; the unit should be the natural service arm of the profitable divisions' installed base.
- **Emergency and response work** — pricing power lives in urgency.
- **Certified or regulated niches** — where entry barriers (accreditations, safety records, OEM authorizations) limit competition.

### 2.3 Where profit typically dies
- **Fixed-price project work won on competitive bid** in oversupplied markets — the classic loss engine.
- **Undifferentiated field labor** where the unit has no scale or footprint advantage.
- **Legacy contracts signed before cost inflation** without escalation clauses — reprice at renewal or exit.
- **The long tail of small, remote, one-off customers** with cost-to-serve above their lifetime margin.

### 2.4 The right-to-win test
A segment or service line stays in the portfolio only if it passes all four:
1. **Positive contribution margin** at steady state, evidenced — not projected on heroic assumptions.
2. **A defensible position:** switching costs, installed base, certifications, or the group channel.
3. **A stable or growing market** at the focused footprint's scale.
4. **No capital requirement the group will not fund.**

### 2.5 The shared-customer question, answered explicitly
Measure margin at group level on shared accounts (unit margin + division margin on the same customer). If group economics are strong but unit economics are thin, fix the transfer pricing so the unit's P&L tells the truth — and recognize that in any exit scenario, these service relationships are the unit's most valuable and most fragile asset. They must be protected or transferred, never stranded.

## 3. The Turnaround Plan — One Year, Four Gates

### Phase 0 — Stabilize (Weeks 0–6)
- **Leadership:** appoint a turnaround lead with full authority and a direct line to the group CEO. If the team proposing the third plan ran the first two, change the leadership or the board should assume the third plan resembles them.
- **Talent:** retention packages for the critical set — the managers the Phase 0 talent map identifies as essential to *any* scenario, including exit. (Order of magnitude: 15–25 in a unit of this kind; the map sets the real number, not a template.) Freeze quiet transfers out — any move becomes a visible, signed decision.
- **Cash:** 13-week rolling cash forecast; capex frozen except safety; aggressive receivables and milestone-billing discipline.
- **Diagnostic** per Section 1.3, with the preliminary verdict at week 8.
- **Narrative:** one honest internal message — one year, one plan, no more surprises.

### Phase 1 — Stop the Bleeding (Months 1–3)
- **Contract triage:** the worst 10–20 contracts are renegotiated, repriced at renewal, or exited. Loss containment on live fixed-price jobs: dedicated project recovery, claims where legitimate.
- **Pricing discipline:** floor pricing, mandatory escalation clauses, a concession-approval matrix. No more buying revenue.
- **Quick revenue:** re-engage shared customers; attach service agreements to sister divisions' installed base.
- **Gate 1 (end of month 3):** diagnostic verdict ratified; focused portfolio defined; **the restated baseline fixed and absolute numeric thresholds set for every later gate** — all subsequent metrics are measured against this restated baseline, or the gates measure accounting artifacts. Cash stabilized; retention secured. *If the verdict is structural (Case C), pivot to exit now — this should normally have surfaced at the week-8 preliminary readout.*

### Phase 2 — Refocus and Restructure, Structurally This Time (Months 3–6)
- **Footprint, not headcount:** close or consolidate depots, branches, and geographies that don't serve the core. The prior restructurings trimmed people; this one removes scope.
- **Start consultation and notification obligations early.** Site closures and tail exits trigger severance, works-council, and statutory notification requirements that in many jurisdictions run for months and gate the calendar. Begin them at Phase 2 outset or they, not the restructuring, will set the pace.
- **Variable-cost model:** subcontract peak load; make-vs-buy reset.
- **Organization redesigned around the focused portfolio** — delayered, with job-level profitability visible weekly.
- **Commercial relaunch:** account plans for the core accounts — the set the matrix shows carries the focused portfolio (order of magnitude: the top 30; the diagnostic sets the real number). Attach-rate and win-rate targets in target segments only.
- **Gate 2 (end of month 6) — the pivot gate:** monthly run-rate losses at least halved *against the restated Gate-1 baseline*; order intake in target segments inflecting upward; tail exits executed; key managers retained. *Miss this gate materially and exit becomes the default path — pre-agreed, not re-litigated.*

### Phase 3 — Prove the Model (Months 6–12)
- **Monthly EBITDA breakeven by month 9–10;** positive run-rate exiting month 12.
- **Backlog coverage rebuilt** in core segments; first renewals signed at new pricing — commercial proof the model holds.
- **Gate 3 (month 9):** board checkpoint — credible path confirmed, or exit execution accelerates.
- **Gate 4 (month 12):** verdict — a business at run-rate profit with a defensible position, or an exit process at the stage defined in Section 4.5.

### 3.1 The milestone table

| Gate | Timing | Hard metrics (all vs. the restated Gate-1 baseline) | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| — | Week 8 | Preliminary diagnostic verdict | Structural case escalates to board immediately |
| 1 | Month 3 | Verdict ratified; portfolio defined; baseline fixed and absolute thresholds set; cash stable; retention secured | Proceed — or exit immediately if structural |
| 2 | Month 6 | Run-rate losses at least halved; core order intake rising; tail exits executed | Continue — or pivot to exit (pre-agreed) |
| 3 | Month 9 | Breakeven in sight month 9–10; renewals at new pricing | Confirm path — or accelerate exit |
| 4 | Month 12 | Positive run-rate; backlog coverage restored | Keep and grow — or exit at the stage defined in 4.5 |

### 3.2 Leading indicators first
The board watches **order intake in target segments, win rate, price realization, utilization, and key-manager retention** monthly — these move quarters before EBITDA does. EBITDA and cash are the lagging confirmation, not the steering wheel.

### 3.3 What this plan explicitly does not do
No acquisitions. No new-market entries. No plan premised on market recovery or heroic win rates. No across-the-board cuts. Those are the moves — and the assumptions — that failed twice.

## 4. Exit Alternatives

### 4.1 The menu

| Option | Best when | Value | Speed/certainty | Key risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Trade sale — whole unit** | A competitor or consolidator covets the installed base and contracts | Potentially highest | Moderate; 6–9 months from launch to signing | Buyers price the shrinking order book, not the history |
| **B. Carve-out sale of the profitable core** + wind-down of the tail | Phase 1 triage separates a clean, sellable core from the losses | Often the value-maximizer | Moderate | Separation complexity; perimeter definition |
| **C. Sponsor sale / MBO** | Cash flows are fixable and fundable under leverage; management will commit | Moderate | Moderate | Financing appetite for a three-year loss-maker |
| **D. Internal transfer to the profitable divisions** | The service capability and shared-customer relationships matter more to the group than standalone value | Captures channel value; protects customers and people | Fast; full control | Not a true exit — the group still owns the economics of the tail |
| **E. Managed wind-down / run-off** | No buyer, no right to win, but contractual backlog to honor | Lowest gross, highest certainty; caps losses | Fully controllable | Stranded costs, employee and customer fallout |
| **F. JV with a stronger operator** | A partner brings the missing capability | Uncertain | Slow — likely beyond the clock | Complexity under time pressure |

### 4.2 Evaluation dimensions
Every option is scored on: **net proceeds after separation costs, stranded costs, one-offs, and the full people cost (4.4); speed and certainty within the clock; impact on shared customers and the profitable divisions; employee outcomes and reputational cost; contractual consents** (change-of-control clauses in service agreements); **residual liabilities** (warranties, retention obligations); and tax.

### 4.3 Separation is the hard part
Shared customers, shared sites, shared systems, and shared people make this a genuine carve-out even in a "simple" sale. Map the entanglement in Phase 1; pre-draft transition service agreements; choreograph customer communication so a sale reads as continuity of service, never as group retreat. The shared-customer relationships are simultaneously the strongest argument for Option D and the biggest risk in Options A–C.

### 4.4 The people cost of exit — costed, not listed
Employee consequences are a line item in the net-proceeds math, not a scoring adjective:
- **Severance and consultation:** cost the severance for every scenario, and map works-council and statutory notification periods by jurisdiction — in several, consultation runs for months and *gates the transaction timeline itself*. An exit triggered at Gate 2 that ignores consultation calendars will miss its own schedule.
- **Retention through the process:** a wind-down or a sale still needs the people who hold customer relationships and know the assets — through closing, not up to it. Budget completion incentives for this group explicitly; losing them mid-process degrades both the asset and the price.
- **The tail exits in Phase 2 carry the same obligations** — they are small versions of Option E, and their people costs belong in the turnaround plan's numbers, not as a later surprise.

### 4.5 Prepare from month 3, decide later — and be honest about the calendar
Build the data room skeleton, carve-out financials, and buyer long-list in parallel with the turnaround, and take quiet banker soundings under NDA. Readiness is cheap; scrambling at month 9 is expensive. Dual-track discipline also improves the turnaround itself — buyer-grade numbers leave nowhere to hide.

Be honest with the board about what the clock can and cannot deliver. A trade sale runs 6–9 months from launch to signing; dual-track preparation compresses the formal process but does not repeal the arithmetic. **The one-year clock decides between a proven turnaround and a committed exit — it does not guarantee a completed one.** Set month-12 expectations by trigger point, now:

| Exit trigger | Process launched | Realistic month-12 state |
|---|---|---|
| Week 8 / Gate 1 (structural) | Month 2–4 | Signed agreement achievable; wind-down well advanced |
| Gate 2 (month 6) | Month 6–7 | LOI or final-round bidders; signing months 12–15; Options D/E can be substantially complete |
| Gate 3 (month 9) | Month 9–10 | Process live, indicative bids in hand; signing months 15–18 |

If the board requires *completion* inside twelve months as opposed to commitment, that constraint itself argues for Options D or E — or for a verdict at week 8 rather than month 9. Say so explicitly at kickoff.

### 4.6 Confidentiality and the leak playbook
The dual track's greatest risk is not buyers saying no — it is the organization finding out. In a unit already losing managers and orders, a rumor of sale accelerates both, potentially killing the turnaround track while degrading the asset being sold.
- **Run it sealed:** code name; a clean team of two to four people plus banker and counsel, firewalled from unit management; need-to-know staging; external soundings limited to a handful under NDA; the data room populated in tranches.
- **Pre-draft the leak response** before it is needed: an honest internal message ("the board is evaluating all options; the turnaround has full support and full funding"), customer reassurance scripts for the top accounts, accelerated retention conversations, and a single spokesperson. A leak handled in hours is a distraction; a leak handled in weeks is a death spiral.
- **Choreograph the real announcement** (per 4.3) as continuity of service — customers and employees hear it from you first, in person where it matters.

---

## 5. The Decision Framework — Turnaround or Divest

### 5.1 Four tests; turnaround must pass all of them
1. **Market test:** the focused core serves a stable or growing market.
2. **Right-to-win test:** a defensible position — channel, installed base, certifications — that competitors cannot easily replicate.
3. **Economics test:** a credible path to positive run-rate EBITDA within 12 months and to the group's hurdle rate thereafter — and probability-weighted turnaround NPV (including required investment *and* the scenario of one more failure) exceeding net exit proceeds.
4. **Capacity test:** the leadership and talent to execute, with confidence honestly discounted for two prior failures.

Fail any one → divest or wind down.

### 5.2 The honest value comparison
Compare probability-weighted NPV of the focused business against sale proceeds net of separation, stranded, and people costs — **both numbers including group-level effects**: the option value of the shared-customer channel on the keep side, and the customer-relationship damage a clumsy sale could inflict on profitable divisions on the exit side.

### 5.3 Bias guards
- **Escalation of commitment** after two restructurings is the default failure mode — which is why gate criteria are fixed with the board now, in writing.
- **Management's incentive skews toward turnaround** (jobs, status, hope). The board owns the exit alternative directly; it is not delegated to the unit.
- **The reverse bias is real too:** a tired group can underinvest in a fixable core and sell at the bottom. The group-level value lens — especially the channel value of shared customers — is the corrective.
- **Option D is not a softer exit; it is a keep decision in disguise.** Internal transfer must clear the same four tests and the same probability-weighted NPV comparison — with the tail's economics included and a named accountable owner in the receiving division. If it cannot, choosing D is deferral, not decision — and it is precisely the option a conflicted management team will reach for to avoid a real one.

### 5.4 Pre-agreed triggers
- Structural verdict at week 8 or Gate 1 → exit immediately.
- Gate 2 metrics missed materially → pivot to exit execution; the dual-track preparation makes this a gear-change, not a scramble.
- The walk-away threshold is set now, before sunk cost accumulates a third time.

---

## 6. Governance and the Board Interface

### 6.1 Decision rights — settled before the work begins
- **The board owns the keep/exit decision.** Gate verdicts are board decisions against the pre-agreed criteria, not management recommendations to be negotiated at the table.
- **A board-level sponsor or transactions committee owns the exit track directly** — outside unit management's reporting line. This operationalizes the bias guard in 5.

## 5. The Decision Framework — Turnaround or Divest

### 5.1 Four tests; turnaround must pass all of them
1. **Market test:** the focused core serves a stable or growing market.
2. **Right-to-win test:** a defensible position — channel, installed base, certifications — that competitors cannot easily replicate.
3. **Economics test:** a credible path to positive run-rate EBITDA within 12 months and to the group's hurdle rate thereafter — and probability-weighted turnaround NPV (including required investment *and* the scenario of one more failure) exceeding net exit proceeds.
4. **Capacity test:** the leadership and talent to execute, with confidence honestly discounted for two prior failures.

Fail any one → divest or wind down.

### 5.2 The honest value comparison
Compare probability-weighted NPV of the focused business against sale proceeds net of separation, stranded, and people costs — **both numbers including group-level effects**: the option value of the shared-customer channel on the keep side, and the customer-relationship damage a clumsy sale could inflict on profitable divisions on the exit side.

### 5.3 Bias guards
- **Escalation of commitment** after two restructurings is the default failure mode — which is why gate criteria are fixed with the board now, in writing.
- **Management's incentive skews toward turnaround** (jobs, status, hope). The board owns the exit alternative directly; it is not delegated to the unit.
- **The reverse bias is real too:** a tired group can underinvest in a fixable core and sell at the bottom. The group-level value lens — especially the channel value of shared customers — is the corrective.
- **Option D is not a softer exit; it is a keep decision in disguise.** Internal transfer must clear the same four tests and the same probability-weighted NPV comparison — with the tail's economics included and a named accountable owner in the receiving division. If it cannot, choosing D is deferral, not decision — and it is precisely the option a conflicted management team will reach for to avoid a real one.

### 5.4 Pre-agreed triggers
- Structural verdict at week 8 or Gate 1 → exit immediately.
- Gate 2 metrics missed materially → pivot to exit execution; the dual-track preparation makes this a gear-change, not a scramble.
- The walk-away threshold is set now, before sunk cost accumulates a third time.

# Fix, Focus, or Exit
## A Turnaround-or-Divestment Assessment and Plan for the Industrial-Services Unit

*Framework for unit leadership, group strategy, and the board. Follows the decision arc: diagnose, focus, prove, decide — under a one-year clock that is not a threat but a discipline. Three years of losses and two failed restructurings are not bad luck; they are data. The third plan cannot be a larger version of the first two.*

---

## Executive Summary

- **The diagnosis in one line:** two cost restructurings that left losses untouched demonstrate that the problem is not overhead — it is what work the unit does, for whom, and at what price. This plan therefore attacks portfolio and revenue quality before it touches cost again.
- **The method:** de-average the P&L to contract level, restate internal work at market prices, and separate a profitable core worth fighting for from a value-destroying tail to be exited. Fix the core; exit the tail. There is no third category.
- **The plan:** a one-year, four-gate turnaround with pre-agreed absolute thresholds, run in parallel with a small, firewalled exit-preparation track — so that a pivot to sale or wind-down at any gate is a gear-change, not a scramble.
- **The decision rule:** turnaround only if the focused core passes four tests — market, right-to-win, economics, execution capacity. Fail any one and the unit is divested or wound down, against criteria fixed in writing before the results arrive.
- **The ask of the board at kickoff:** sign the one-page charter (gate criteria, decision rights, month-12 exit expectations); appoint the turnaround lead and the board sponsor who owns the exit track; fund both tracks properly.

## 0. Operating Principles

1. **Two failed cost restructurings are the diagnosis's first clue.** Costs were cut and losses persisted — which means the problem lives in revenue quality, portfolio mix, or structural position, not in overhead. You cannot cut your way to profit on a deteriorating top line.
2. **De-average everything.** The blended P&L conceals a profitable core and a value-destroying tail. Every decision in this plan is made at the level of service line × customer segment × contract, never at unit level.
3. **Talent flight is a vote, and the voters have the best information.** The managers transferring out are the ones with options. Decode why they're leaving before writing the plan — and stop the outflow, because no plan survives the loss of the people meant to execute it.
4. **Evaluate everything at group level.** The unit serves customers of the profitable divisions. Its failure can damage relationships it doesn't own; its service capability may be worth more to the group than its standalone P&L shows. Every option — fix, sell, close — is priced including effects on sister divisions.
5. **Run turnaround and exit in parallel — and quietly.** The one-year clock forbids sequencing. Dual-track preparation preserves optionality and imposes buyer-grade discipline on the turnaround numbers. But a leaked sale process inside a fragile organization accelerates the very talent flight and customer defection that are already the unit's biggest problems. The exit track runs small, firewalled, and under a code name until a gate forces it open.
6. **Define "credible" before the results arrive.** Agree now, in writing, what a credible path to profitability looks like at each gate — measured against a restated baseline, with absolute thresholds. Otherwise the month-12 debate will be politics, not analysis — and sunk cost will argue for a fourth year.

## 1. Diagnostic — Structural or Execution?

### 1.1 The tests that distinguish them

| Test | Question | Evidence of structural failure | Evidence of execution failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Market** | Is the served market growing, flat, or declining? | End markets in secular decline; technology displacing the service | Market stable/growing; competitors adding capacity |
| **Relative economics** | Are competitors profitable in the same segments? | No one makes money; industry-wide margin collapse | Named competitors earn acceptable margins on comparable work |
| **Order book** | Why is it shrinking — lost bids, lost customers, or shrinking customer demand? | Customers' own demand is falling; work is being in-sourced or obsoleted | Win rates falling on bids we should win; churn to specific rivals |
| **Cost position** | Landed cost vs. competitors at equal scope | Structural disadvantage: scale, footprint, labor agreements, asset age | Utilization, scheduling, and rework problems — fixable with management |
| **Contract quality** | Where does margin leak? | Whole categories priced below cost by the market | Specific fixed-price jobs overrun; escalation clauses missing; pricing undisciplined |
| **Transfer pricing** | What does the P&L look like at market prices for work done for sister divisions? | — | Losses concentrated in internal work at non-market internal prices — an artifact, not a business failure |

### 1.2 Reading the known facts
- **Cost cuts that didn't touch losses** point to a revenue-mix or structural problem. The first question is not "where else can we cut" but "which work should we be doing at all."
- **A shrinking order book** is a demand-side signal. It must be decomposed: market decline (structural), competitive losses (execution — unless they persist for three years, in which case they usually reflect a structural disadvantage in scale, footprint, or capability), or deliberate low-ball bidding by rivals buying share.
- **Management flight** is both symptom and cause. It signals collapsed internal confidence and steadily erodes the execution capacity any turnaround depends on. Exit interviews with departed managers are a diagnostic instrument — use them.
- **The shared-customer overlap cuts both ways.** If the unit cannot profitably serve customers already buying from sister divisions, either execution is badly broken or the unit is being used as a margin sink for group deals at internal prices. Audit transfer pricing before concluding anything — the unit's "losses" may partly be an accounting artifact, and its true market-price economics may be better (or worse) than reported.

### 1.3 The diagnostic workplan (weeks 1–6, verdict at week 8)
- **Contract-level P&L:** rebuild three years of results contract by contract — price, cost, overruns, escalation terms. The order book gets the same treatment: which backlog is actually profitable at completion?
- **Win/loss and churn analysis** on 24 months of bids; interviews with the top 20 customers, including defectors.
- **Competitor benchmarking:** cost position, pricing, and profitability of two or three named rivals.
- **Transfer-pricing audit** of all work for sister divisions, restated at market rates — this restated P&L becomes the baseline for every gate metric in the plan.
- **Exit interviews** with every manager who transferred out in 24 months.
- **Preliminary verdict to the board at week 8.** A structural finding (Case C below) goes to the board then — not at Gate 1. No one burns four extra months confirming a verdict that is already clear.

### 1.4 The four possible verdicts
- **A — Healthy market, broken execution:** turnaround is credible; proceed to Section 3 in full.
- **B — Declining market, defensible niche:** shrink-to-profit — exit the broad market, concentrate on the protected niche.
- **C — Structural disadvantage, no right to win:** go directly to exit (Section 4). Do not burn nine months confirming it.
- **D — Mixed portfolio (the most likely):** fix the core, exit the tail — the plan below is built for this case.

## 2. Where Profit Can Live — Segments and Service Lines

### 2.1 Build the matrix
Construct a service-line × customer-segment profitability matrix at two levels: contribution margin and fully loaded cost, with internal work restated at market prices. Rank every cell. The plan concentrates on the top cells and exits the bottom ones — there is no third category.

### 2.2 Hypotheses to validate — where profit typically survives
- **Recurring-revenue service agreements** tied to an installed base — predictable, defensible, priced on value rather than bid.
- **Work for shared group customers at market pricing** — a channel advantage no competitor has; the unit should be the natural service arm of the profitable divisions' installed base.
- **Emergency and response work** — pricing power lives in urgency.
- **Certified or regulated niches** — where entry barriers (accreditations, safety records, OEM authorizations) limit competition.

### 2.3 Where profit typically dies
- **Fixed-price project work won on competitive bid** in oversupplied markets — the classic loss engine.
- **Undifferentiated field labor** where the unit has no scale or footprint advantage.
- **Legacy contracts signed before cost inflation** without escalation clauses — reprice at renewal or exit.
- **The long tail of small, remote, one-off customers** with cost-to-serve above their lifetime margin.

### 2.4 The right-to-win test
A segment or service line stays in the portfolio only if it passes all four:
1. **Positive contribution margin** at steady state, evidenced — not projected on heroic assumptions.
2. **A defensible position:** switching costs, installed base, certifications, or the group channel.
3. **A stable or growing market** at the focused footprint's scale.
4. **No capital requirement the group will not fund.**

### 2.5 The shared-customer question, answered explicitly
Measure margin at group level on shared accounts (unit margin + division margin on the same customer). If group economics are strong but unit economics are thin, fix the transfer pricing so the unit's P&L tells the truth — and recognize that in any exit scenario, these service relationships are the unit's most valuable and most fragile asset. They must be protected or transferred, never stranded.

Measure margin at group level on shared accounts (unit margin + division margin on the same customer). If group economics are strong but unit economics are thin, fix the transfer pricing so the unit's P&L tells the truth — and recognize that in any exit scenario, these service relationships are the unit's most valuable and most fragile asset. They must be protected or transferred, never stranded.

## 3. The Turnaround Plan — One Year, Four Gates

### Phase 0 — Stabilize (Weeks 0–6)
- **Leadership:** appoint a turnaround lead with full authority and a direct line to the group CEO. If the team proposing the third plan ran the first two, change the leadership or the board should assume the third plan resembles them.
- **Talent:** retention packages for the critical set — the managers the Phase 0 talent map identifies as essential to *any* scenario, including exit. (Order of magnitude: 15–25 in a unit of this kind; the map sets the real number, not a template.) Freeze quiet transfers out — any move becomes a visible, signed decision.
- **Cash:** 13-week rolling cash forecast; capex frozen except safety; aggressive receivables and milestone-billing discipline.
- **Diagnostic** per Section 1.3, with the preliminary verdict at week 8.
- **Narrative:** one honest internal message — one year, one plan, no more surprises.

### Phase 1 — Stop the Bleeding (Months 1–3)
- **Contract triage:** the worst 10–20 contracts are renegotiated, repriced at renewal, or exited. Loss containment on live fixed-price jobs: dedicated project recovery, claims where legitimate.
- **Pricing discipline:** floor pricing, mandatory escalation clauses, a concession-approval matrix. No more buying revenue.
- **Quick revenue:** re-engage shared customers; attach service agreements to sister divisions' installed base.
- **Gate 1 (end of month 3):** diagnostic verdict ratified; focused portfolio defined; **the restated baseline fixed and absolute numeric thresholds set for every later gate** — all subsequent metrics are measured against this restated baseline, or the gates measure accounting artifacts. Cash stabilized; retention secured. *If the verdict is structural (Case C), pivot to exit now — this should normally have surfaced at the week-8 preliminary readout.*

### Phase 2 — Refocus and Restructure, Structurally This Time (Months 3–6)
- **Footprint, not headcount:** close or consolidate depots, branches, and geographies that don't serve the core. The prior restructurings trimmed people; this one removes scope.
- **Start consultation and notification obligations early.** Site closures and tail exits trigger severance, works-council, and statutory notification requirements that in many jurisdictions run for months and gate the calendar. Begin them at Phase 2 outset or they, not the restructuring, will set the pace.
- **Variable-cost model:** subcontract peak load; make-vs-buy reset.
- **Organization redesigned around the focused portfolio** — delayered, with job-level profitability visible weekly.
- **Commercial relaunch:** account plans for the core accounts — the set the matrix shows carries the focused portfolio (order of magnitude: the top 30; the diagnostic sets the real number). Attach-rate and win-rate targets in target segments only.
- **Gate 2 (end of month 6) — the pivot gate:** monthly run-rate losses at least halved *against the restated Gate-1 baseline*; order intake in target segments inflecting upward; tail exits executed; key managers retained. *Miss this gate materially and exit becomes the default path — pre-agreed, not re-litigated.*

### Phase 3 — Prove the Model (Months 6–12)
- **Monthly EBITDA breakeven by month 9–10;** positive run-rate exiting month 12.
- **Backlog coverage rebuilt** in core segments; first renewals signed at new pricing — commercial proof the model holds.
- **Gate 3 (month 9):** board checkpoint — credible path confirmed, or exit execution accelerates.
- **Gate 4 (month 12):** verdict — a business at run-rate profit with a defensible position, or an exit process at the stage defined in Section 4.5.

### 3.1 The milestone table

| Gate | Timing | Hard metrics (all vs. the restated Gate-1 baseline) | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| — | Week 8 | Preliminary diagnostic verdict | Structural case escalates to board immediately |
| 1 | Month 3 | Verdict ratified; portfolio defined; baseline fixed and absolute thresholds set; cash stable; retention secured | Proceed — or exit immediately if structural |

### 3.2 Leading indicators first
The board watches **order intake in target segments, win rate, price realization, utilization, and key-manager retention** monthly — these move quarters before EBITDA does. EBITDA and cash are the lagging confirmation, not the steering wheel.

### 3.3 What this plan explicitly does not do
No acquisitions. No new-market entries. No plan premised on market recovery or heroic win rates. No across-the-board cuts. Those are the moves — and the assumptions — that failed twice.

## 4. Exit Alternatives

### 4.1 The menu

| Option | Best when | Value | Speed/certainty | Key risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Trade sale — whole unit** | A competitor or consolidator covets the installed base and contracts | Potentially highest | Moderate; 6–9 months from launch to signing | Buyers price the shrinking order book, not the history |
| **B. Carve-out sale of the profitable core** + wind-down of the tail | Phase 1 triage separates a clean, sellable core from the losses | Often the value-maximizer | Moderate | Separation complexity; perimeter definition |
| **C. Sponsor sale / MBO** | Cash flows are fixable and fundable under leverage; management will commit | Moderate | Moderate | Financing appetite for a three-year loss-maker |
| **D. Internal transfer to the profitable divisions** | The service capability and shared-customer relationships matter more to the group than standalone value | Captures channel value; protects customers and people | Fast; full control | Not a true exit — the group still owns the economics of the tail |
| **E. Managed wind-down / run-off** | No buyer, no right to win, but contractual backlog to honor | Lowest gross, highest certainty; caps losses | Fully controllable | Stranded costs, employee and customer fallout |
| **F. JV with a stronger operator** | A partner brings the missing capability | Uncertain | Slow — likely beyond the clock | Complexity under time pressure |

### 4.2 Evaluation dimensions
Every option is scored on: **net proceeds after separation costs, stranded costs, one-offs, and the full people cost (4.4); speed and certainty within the clock; impact on shared customers and the profitable divisions; employee outcomes and reputational cost; contractual consents** (change-of-control clauses in service agreements); **residual liabilities** (warranties, retention obligations); and tax.

### 4.3 Separation is the hard part
Shared customers, shared sites, shared systems, and shared people make this a genuine carve-out even in a "simple" sale. Map the entanglement in Phase 1; pre-draft transition service agreements; choreograph customer communication so a sale reads as continuity of service, never as group retreat. The shared-customer relationships are simultaneously the strongest argument for Option D and the biggest risk in Options A–C.

### 4.4 The people cost of exit — costed, not listed
Employee consequences are a line item in the net-proceeds math, not a scoring adjective:
- **Severance and consultation:** cost the severance for every scenario, and map works-council and statutory notification periods by jurisdiction — in several, consultation runs for months and *gates the transaction timeline itself*. An exit triggered at Gate 2 that ignores consultation calendars will miss its own schedule.
- **Retention through the process:** a wind-down or a sale still needs the people who hold customer relationships and know the assets — through closing, not up to it. Budget completion incentives for this group explicitly; losing them mid-process degrades both the asset and the price.
- **The tail exits in Phase 2 carry the same obligations** — they are small versions of Option E, and their people costs belong in the turnaround plan's numbers, not as a later surprise.

### 4.5 Prepare from month 3, decide later — and be honest about the calendar
Build the data room skeleton, carve-out financials, and buyer long-list in parallel with the turnaround, and take quiet banker soundings under NDA. Readiness is cheap; scrambling at month 9 is expensive. Dual-track discipline also improves the turnaround itself — buyer-grade numbers leave nowhere to hide.

Be honest with the board about what the clock can and cannot deliver. A trade sale runs 6–9 months from launch to signing; dual-track preparation compresses the formal process but does not repeal the arithmetic. **The one-year clock decides between a proven turnaround and a committed exit — it does not guarantee a completed one.** Set month-12 expectations by trigger point, now:

| Exit trigger | Process launched | Realistic month-12 state |
|---|---|---|
| Week 8 / Gate 1 (structural) | Month 2–4 | Signed agreement achievable; wind-down well advanced |
| Gate 2 (month 6) | Month 6–7 | LOI or final-round bidders; signing months 12–15; Options D/E can be substantially complete |
| Gate 3 (month 9) | Month 9–10 | Process live, indicative bids in hand; signing months 15–18 |

If the board requires *completion* inside twelve months as opposed to commitment, that constraint itself argues for Options D or E — or for a verdict at week 8 rather than month 9. Say so explicitly at kickoff.

### 4.6 Confidentiality and the leak playbook
The dual track's greatest risk is not buyers saying no — it is the organization finding out. In a unit already losing managers and orders, a rumor of sale accelerates both, potentially killing the turnaround track while degrading the asset being sold.
- **Run it sealed:** code name; a clean team of two to four people plus banker and counsel, firewalled from unit management; need-to-know staging; external soundings limited to a handful under NDA; the data room populated in tranches.
- **Pre-draft the leak response** before it is needed: an honest internal message ("the board is evaluating all options; the turnaround has full support and full funding"), customer reassurance scripts for the top accounts, accelerated retention conversations, and a single spokesperson. A leak handled in hours is a distraction; a leak handled in weeks is a death spiral.
- **Choreograph the real announcement** (per 4.3) as continuity of service — customers and employees hear it from you first, in person where it matters.

## 5. The Decision Framework — Turnaround or Divest

### 5.1 Four tests; turnaround must pass all of them
1. **Market test:** the focused core serves a stable or growing market.
2. **Right-to-win test:** a defensible position — channel, installed base, certifications — that competitors cannot easily replicate.
3. **Economics test:** a credible path to positive run-rate EBITDA within 12 months and to the group's hurdle rate thereafter — and probability-weighted turnaround NPV (including required investment *and* the scenario of one more failure) exceeding net exit proceeds.
4. **Capacity test:** the leadership and talent to execute, with confidence honestly discounted for two prior failures.

Fail any one → divest or wind down.

### 5.2 The honest value comparison
Compare probability-weighted NPV of the focused business against sale proceeds net of separation, stranded, and people costs — **both numbers including group-level effects**: the option value of the shared-customer channel on the keep side, and the customer-relationship damage a clumsy sale could inflict on profitable divisions on the exit side.

### 5.3 Bias guards
- **Escalation of commitment** after two restructurings is the default failure mode — which is why gate criteria are fixed with the board now, in writing.
- **Management's incentive skews toward turnaround** (jobs, status, hope). The board owns the exit alternative directly; it is not delegated to the unit.
- **The reverse bias is real too:** a tired group can underinvest in a fixable core and sell at the bottom. The group-level value lens — especially the channel value of shared customers — is the corrective.
- **Option D is not a softer exit; it is a keep decision in disguise.** Internal transfer must clear the same four tests and the same probability-weighted NPV comparison — with the tail's economics included and a named accountable owner in the receiving division. If it cannot, choosing D is deferral, not decision — and it is precisely the option a conflicted management team will reach for to avoid a real one.

### 5.4 Pre-agreed triggers
- Structural verdict at week 8 or Gate 1 → exit immediately.
- Gate 2 metrics missed materially → pivot to exit execution; the dual-track preparation makes this a gear-change, not a scramble.
- The walk-away threshold is set now, before sunk cost accumulates a third time.

- **A board-level sponsor or transactions committee owns the exit track directly** — outside unit management's reporting line. This operationalizes the bias guard in 5.

# Fix, Focus, or Exit
## A Turnaround-or-Divestment Assessment and Plan for the Industrial-Services Unit

*Framework for unit leadership, group strategy, and the board. Follows the decision arc: diagnose, focus, prove, decide — under a one-year clock that is not a threat but a discipline. Three years of losses and two failed restructurings are not bad luck; they are data. The third plan cannot be a larger version of the first two.*

---

## Executive Summary

- **The diagnosis in one line:** two cost restructurings that left losses untouched demonstrate that the problem is not overhead — it is what work the unit does, for whom, and at what price. This plan therefore attacks portfolio and revenue quality before it touches cost again.
- **The method:** de-average the P&L to contract level, restate internal work at market prices, and dissect the two prior plans before writing the third. The diagnostic has four verdicts — from fix-all (rare) to exit-all (structural) — but the center of gravity is fix the core, exit the tail.
- **The plan:** a one-year, four-gate turnaround with pre-agreed absolute thresholds, precisely defined metrics, and a cost-to-achieve envelope approved by the board — run in parallel with a small, firewalled exit-preparation track, so that a pivot to sale or wind-down at any gate is a gear-change, not a scramble.
- **The decision rule:** turnaround only if the focused core passes four tests — market, right-to-win, economics, execution capacity. Fail any one and the unit is divested or wound down, against criteria fixed in writing before the results arrive.
- **The ask of the board at kickoff:** sign the one-page charter (gate criteria, decision rights, month-12 exit expectations, cost-to-achieve cap with tranche release); appoint the turnaround lead and the board sponsor who owns the exit track; fund both tracks properly.

---

## 0. Operating Principles

1. **Two failed cost restructurings are the diagnosis's first clue.** Costs were cut and losses persisted — which means the problem lives in revenue quality, portfolio mix, or structural position, not in overhead. You cannot cut your way to profit on a deteriorating top line.
2. **De-average everything.** The blended P&L conceals a profitable core and a value-destroying tail. Every decision in this plan is made at the level of service line × customer segment × contract, never at unit level.
3. **Talent flight is a vote, and the voters have the best information.** The managers transferring out are the ones with options. Decode why they're leaving before writing the plan — and stop the outflow by making staying attractive, not by making leaving hard. No plan survives the loss of the people meant to execute it.
4. **Evaluate everything at group level.** The unit serves customers of the profitable divisions. Its failure can damage relationships it doesn't own; its service capability may be worth more to the group than its standalone P&L shows. Every option — fix, sell, close — is priced including effects on sister divisions.
5. **Run turnaround and exit in parallel — and quietly.** The one-year clock forbids sequencing. Dual-track preparation preserves optionality and imposes buyer-grade discipline on the turnaround numbers. But a leaked sale process inside a fragile organization accelerates the very talent flight and customer defection that are already the unit's biggest problems. The exit track runs small, firewalled, and under a code name until a gate forces it open.
6. **Define "credible" before the results arrive.** Agree now, in writing, what a credible path to profitability looks like at each gate — measured against a restated baseline, with absolute thresholds and fixed measurement conventions. Otherwise the month-12 debate will be politics, not analysis — and sunk cost will argue for a fourth year.

## 1. Diagnostic — Structural or Execution?

### 1.1 The tests that distinguish them

| Test | Question | Evidence of structural failure | Evidence of execution failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Market** | Is the served market growing, flat, or declining? | End markets in secular decline; technology displacing the service | Market stable/growing; competitors adding capacity |
| **Relative economics** | Are competitors profitable in the same segments? | No one makes money; industry-wide margin collapse | Named competitors earn acceptable margins on comparable work |
| **Order book** | Why is it shrinking — lost bids, lost customers, or shrinking customer demand? | Customers' own demand is falling; work is being in-sourced or obsoleted | Win rates falling on bids we should win; churn to specific rivals |
| **Cost position** | Landed cost vs. competitors at equal scope | Structural disadvantage: scale, footprint, labor agreements, asset age | Utilization, scheduling, and rework problems — fixable with management |
| **Contract quality** | Where does margin leak? | Whole categories priced below cost by the market | Specific fixed-price jobs overrun; escalation clauses missing; pricing undisciplined |
| **Transfer pricing** | What does the P&L look like at market prices for work done for sister divisions? | — | Losses concentrated in internal work at non-market internal prices — an artifact, not a business failure |

### 1.2 Reading the known facts
- **Cost cuts that didn't touch losses** point to a revenue-mix or structural problem. The first question is not "where else can we cut" but "which work should we be doing at all."
- **A shrinking order book** is a demand-side signal. It must be decomposed: market decline (structural), competitive losses (execution — unless they persist for three years, in which case they usually reflect a structural disadvantage in scale, footprint, or capability), or deliberate low-ball bidding by rivals buying share.
- **Management flight** is both symptom and cause. It signals collapsed internal confidence and steadily erodes the execution capacity any turnaround depends on. Exit interviews with departed managers are a diagnostic instrument — use them.
- **The shared-customer overlap cuts both ways.** If the unit cannot profitably serve customers already buying from sister divisions, either execution is badly broken or the unit is being used as a margin sink for group deals at internal prices. Audit transfer pricing before concluding anything — the unit's "losses" may partly be an accounting artifact, and its true market-price economics may be better (or worse) than reported.

### 1.3 The plan-zero post-mortem (weeks 1–4)
Before designing the third plan, dissect the first two. This is a formal workstream, not a conversation.
- **Reconstruct the prior plans' written assumptions** — volumes, price realization, mix, savings, timing, market outlook — and compare each against what actually happened, line by line.
- **Ask three questions of every failed assumption:** Was it knowably wrong at the time (an honesty failure) or genuinely unforecastable (a forecasting failure)? Who produced it, and through what process? Is any version of it present in the current plan?
- **Produce the output as a one-page "forbidden assumptions" list,** signed by the turnaround lead and presented with the week-8 verdict. Every material assumption in the new plan is checked against it.
- **The post-mortem is also the evidence base for the capacity test in 5.1.** A team that cannot explain why its last two plans failed has not earned the right to run the third.

### 1.4 The diagnostic workplan (weeks 1–6, verdict at week 8)
- **Contract-level P&L:** rebuild three years of results contract by contract — price, cost, overruns, escalation terms. The order book gets the same treatment: which backlog is actually profitable at completion?
- **Win/loss and churn analysis** on 24 months of bids; interviews with the top 20 customers, including defectors.
- **Competitor benchmarking:** cost position, pricing, and profitability of two or three named rivals.
- **Transfer-pricing audit** of all work for sister divisions, restated at market rates — this restated P&L becomes the baseline for every gate metric in the plan.
- **Exit interviews** with every manager who transferred out in 24 months.
- **Plan-zero post-mortem** per 1.3.
- **Preliminary verdict to the board at week 8.** A structural finding (Case C in 1.5) goes to the board then — not at Gate 1. No one burns four extra months confirming a verdict that is already clear.

### 1.5 The four possible verdicts
- **A — Healthy market, broken execution:** turnaround is credible; proceed to Section 3 in full.
- **B — Declining market, defensible niche:** shrink-to-profit — exit the broad market, concentrate on the protected niche.
- **C — Structural disadvantage, no right to win:** go directly to exit (Section 4). Do not burn nine months confirming it.
- **D — Mixed portfolio (the most likely):** fix the core, exit the tail — the plan below is built for this case.
